analysis.one_liner: Requires presidential candidates to release 20 years of tax returns and bans federal spending that profits the President's own businesses.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote: with zero cosponsors, it sat in three House committees until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required anyone running for President or Vice President to disclose 20 years of tax returns, barred the government from paying for events or lodging at businesses owned by the President, Vice President, or any federal employee, banned government contractors from donating to inaugural committees, and extended ethics and nepotism rules to the White House staff. It was introduced by one member, attracted no cosponsors, was sent to three House committees, and died there without a single hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday taxpayers and voters. They would gain visibility into presidential candidates' financial conflicts of interest, stop taxpayer money from enriching a sitting President's private businesses, and see public quarterly reports on officials' use of government aircraft. Honest government contractors would also benefit from competitors being barred from donating to inaugural committees.

how_it_helps.text: Requires presidential and vice-presidential candidates to disclose 20 years of tax returns, with the Office of Government Ethics allowed to publish them — closing a gap left when Donald Trump broke decades of voluntary release, though the bill text does not name him.

Bars federal funds from being spent at any property owned by the President, Vice President, or any federal employee when the payment profits that person's family — aimed at government spending at Trump-owned hotels and resorts.

Extends the anti-nepotism statute to the White House and Executive Office of the President and adds a $1,000-a-day fine for violating it, aimed at family members holding White House jobs (Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, though not named).
Requires quarterly public reports on officials' use of government aircraft, including the reason and estimated cost, published on GSA's website.
Bars government contractors from donating to presidential inaugural committees, and requires disclosure of who funds officials' legal defense funds.

analysis.who_pays: Sitting Presidents, Vice Presidents, and federal employees whose businesses would lose the ability to collect federal payments, and whose family members could no longer take White House jobs. Political candidates with complex private finances would face mandatory 20-year tax disclosure, and inaugural committees would lose contractor money.

drawbacks.text: Requiring 20 years of tax returns from presidential candidates is contested on privacy grounds; the bill's own text acknowledges this by allowing redaction of personal information to prevent identity theft or physical danger — an acknowledgment that disclosure carries real risks.

Some provisions take blunt instruments: the bill bans all reimbursement of an executive employee's legal fees except from relatives or OGE-approved funds, which could leave lower-paid employees facing personal legal costs from their jobs with no help, and the $1,000-per-day nepotism fine attaches to the appointed employee as well as the official, including career employees.

The bill would extend the Hatch Act and ethics-reporting regime squarely into the White House and Executive Office of the President, which Presidents of both parties have historically resisted as intruding on the President's control of their own staff.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are meaningful: presidential and vice-presidential tax disclosure, an end to taxpayer money flowing to officials' own businesses, and penalties for nepotism at the White House. The costs are minimal — some compliance burden and a strong argument from officials' side that disclosure requirements should be narrower — but the bill was never examined in a hearing or marked up, so its practical design was never tested. It died without opposition being recorded, which makes the cost side largely unexamined rather than known to be serious.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Oversight, House Administration, and Ways and Means committees the day it was introduced, and no committee ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 6, 2019 and referred to three committees: Oversight and Reform, House Administration, and Ways and Means.
It drew zero cosponsors in the House.
The action history records no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no Senate companion activity after the referral.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and all bills not passed expire with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Presidential administrations and their family businesses, which would have faced mandatory tax disclosure, nepotism fines, and a ban on federal spending at their properties, keep the status quo. The bill also never disturbed existing inaugural-committee fundraising from contractors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sitting administrations and their family businesses

for.name: Rep. Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no committee action followed.

against.name: President Donald Trump
against.what_they_did: Was the sitting President whose refusal to release tax returns, family members' White House roles, and family-owned hotels were the bill's clear targets; his administration set the environment in which no House committee took up the bill.

against.name: House committees (Oversight and Reform, House Administration, Ways and Means)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no record shows where members stood.

industries.industry: Hospitality and hotel operators that lease space to the federal government (notably properties owned by sitting officeholders)
industries.note: The bill would bar federal money from being spent at properties that financially benefit the President, the Vice President, or any federal employee or their family. This was aimed at the Trump Organization's hotel business, which had been receiving payments for government events and lodging.

Contractors would be barred from donating to presidential inaugural committees, closing a channel where contractors could buy visibility and goodwill with a new administration. The public benefit is a reduced appearance of pay-to-play.

industries.industry: Law firms and legal-fee fund organizers
industries.note: The bill bans most reimbursement of executive-branch officials' legal fees and imposes strict disclosure and approval rules on legal expense funds, shrinking a niche market while adding compliance rules for the remainder.
